slides.title: Question
slides.notes: Open by naming the chapter question rather than the theorem first. The source span wants a first heuristic proof, so the lecture should make the invariant visible before stating the final global formula. A plane loop is the smallest laboratory: it can bend, stretch, and develop inflection points, but the tangent direction still carries an integer degree as long as the loop remains regular.

slides.title: Route
slides.notes: Use this route slide as a contract with the audience. The proof is not a black-box integration trick. It is a migration of one idea: count how a direction map covers its target. First the target is the circle of tangent directions for a plane loop. Then the same count becomes normal direction on a surface, and finally the count becomes Euler characteristic through cell-like bookkeeping.

slides.title: Turning Degree
slides.notes: Slow down on the map T:S1 to S1. The domain circle is the curve parameter after one full trip; the target circle is the set of possible unit tangent directions. The integral of signed curvature measures angular velocity of this target point. Hopf's statement is therefore a degree statement: for a simple positive loop, the tangent direction makes one full positive lap.

slides.title: Inflections
slides.notes: This is the place to prevent a common misconception: positive curvature everywhere is not the invariant. A circle has that convenient property, but deformations can introduce arcs with the opposite sign. The invariant is the total angular change of the tangent direction. As long as the tangent vector never vanishes and the map remains continuous, the degree cannot slide continuously from one integer to another.

slides.title: Proof State
slides.notes: Present this slide as the logical core of the chapter's first half. We are not claiming every drawing preserves the invariant by visual resemblance. We are claiming that a regular deformation gives a continuous family of maps into the circle, and degree is integer-valued. The only way to change it is to pass through a state where the tangent map is not defined or no longer belongs to the same class.

slides.title: Surface Transfer
slides.notes: Make the analogy explicit. For curves, the tangent map sends each point of the loop to a direction on the unit circle, and signed curvature is angular change. For surfaces, the Gauss map sends each point to a unit normal on the sphere, and Gaussian curvature is the signed area distortion of that map. This is the geometric reason an integral of K dA can count covering behavior.

slides.title: Global Formula
slides.notes: State the global theorem as the destination of the analogy, but keep the word heuristic honest. The chapter's route is visual: total curvature is the signed area swept out by normals, and the global count depends on the surface's topological type. The notebook ledger records the sample values 4 pi, 0, -4 pi, and -8 pi for Euler characteristics 2, 0, -2, and -4.

slides.title: Bookkeeping
slides.notes: This slide explains why the answer is not merely a normal-map area. When a surface is decomposed into small pieces, each boundary has its own turning contribution. Shared edges are traversed in opposite directions by adjacent pieces, so their boundary bookkeeping cancels. What remains is concentrated at corners or defects, and the surviving count has the Euler-characteristic pattern V minus E plus F.

slides.title: Lab
slides.notes: Use this slide to connect lecture proof habits to the notebook. The student task is not to admire a curve picture; it is to name the parameter, name the invariant, and state the singular event that would change the answer. The check files make that discipline concrete by recording nonblank artifacts, Euler-characteristic totals, limiting behavior, and orientation-sensitive wedge products.

slides.title: Recap
slides.notes: Close by compressing the proof without pretending it is fully rigorous. The students should leave with the analogy between tangent degree and normal-map degree, plus the cancellation habit that makes Euler characteristic appear. The final sentence is the reusable method for later differential geometry: representations can bend and change coordinates, but a valid invariant survives exactly because the proof has excluded the events that would destroy it.
